lesson.title: Who else is watching?
lesson.subtitle: Wi-Fi, trackers and your data trail

video.title: Who else is watching?
video.format_note: Animated explainer for students aged 12–16, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello — the student's form teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Amina at a cyber café beside a student using her phone on the café's Wi-Fi; a Wi-Fi sign hangs over the owner's desk.
scenes.animation: Wi-Fi waves pulse from the router to every screen.
scenes.narration: At a cyber café, a student using the free Wi-Fi on her phone asked me, “Can the owner see my messages?” Good question. Let's find out who else can see what you do online, and how to share less.

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the cyber track chip.
scenes.narration: Today: Wi-Fi, trackers, and the data trail you leave without noticing.

scenes.visual: A router in the middle; lines run from phones to websites through it; three possible owners stand beside it: a café owner, a school office, a shadowy stranger with a fake sign.
scenes.animation: Each owner pops in as named.
scenes.on_screen_text: The network sees where you go
scenes.narration: When you use a Wi-Fi network, whoever runs it can see which websites and apps you use, and when. That could be the café owner, the school, or a stranger who set up a fake hotspot with a friendly name.

scenes.visual: A web address with a padlock; the message inside an envelope turns into scrambled letters as it passes the router.
scenes.animation: Letters scramble as the envelope passes.
scenes.narration: That's why the padlock matters. With HTTPS, what you type and read is scrambled on its way. The network can still see which site you visit, but not your password or your messages. And chat apps with end-to-end encryption keep your messages unreadable to the café.

scenes.visual: A cartoon invisibility cloak labelled 'private browsing' slips off; the router can still see the student.
scenes.narration: Private browsing sounds like a cloak of invisibility, but it isn't. It only stops this phone from saving your history and cookies. The Wi-Fi network, your school and the websites can still see you.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina holds up a phone in a private browsing window, beside the café's router.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Does private browsing hide what you do from the café's Wi-Fi?

scenes.visual: The 'no' card gets the check badge; a family phone shows an empty history list.
scenes.narration: No. It only keeps your history off this phone, which is useful on a shared or family phone.

scenes.visual: A student looks at a pair of trainers once; small eye icons follow her from site to site; trainer adverts appear everywhere.
scenes.animation: Eyes hop from page to page; adverts pop up.
scenes.narration: Then there are trackers: small pieces of code on websites and in apps. They follow you from site to site and build a profile of what you like, to show you adverts. That's why you look at trainers once and see trainers everywhere for a week.

scenes.visual: A free bus; on board, a man with a notebook writes down where every passenger gets off.
scenes.narration: Many free apps are like a free bus ride with someone on board writing down where everyone goes. You don't pay with money. You pay with information about yourself.

scenes.visual: A privacy settings screen; switches turn off one by one; an unused app is dragged to the bin.
scenes.animation: Switches flip as they are named.
scenes.narration: You can share less. Make your accounts private, and choose who can message you. Turn off ad personalisation and location history in your settings. And delete apps you no longer use, because some keep collecting.

scenes.visual: Ms Amina at a bus station, phone in hand, under a 'Free Wi-Fi' sign.
scenes.narration: Your turn. On the bus station's free Wi-Fi, which is safer: reading the football news, or signing in to pay with mobile money?

scenes.visual: The 'football news' card gets the check badge, then four summary cards line up.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right.
scenes.narration: Reading the news, because signing in and paying can wait for mobile data or a network you trust. Remember: the network sees where you go, the padlock hides what's inside, private browsing only protects this phone, and trackers turn your clicks into adverts.

scenes.visual: A student opens an app's privacy settings and switches one setting off, then shows a friend.
scenes.animation: A switch flips off; a chat bubble appears.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: open the privacy settings of one app you use every day. Turn off one thing you didn't know was on, and tell a friend what you found.

checkpoints.prompt: Does private browsing hide what you do from the café's Wi-Fi?

options.text: No — it only stops this phone saving your history

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the network and the websites still see you. Private browsing only keeps your history off this phone.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — private browsing only stops this phone saving your history and cookies. The café's network can still see which sites you visit.

checkpoints.prompt: On the bus station's free Wi-Fi, which is safer?

options.text: Signing in to pay with mobile money

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — reading is fine. Sign in and pay on mobile data or a network you trust.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a free network may be fake or watched. Sign in and pay only on mobile data or a network you trust.
